title: Comparison between color doppler ultrasound-guided and conventionally ultrasound-guided nerve catheter placement at the interscalene brachial plexus for major shoulder surgeries regarding perioperative pain, mobilization, procedural times, and peri-procedural complications.
summary:
This scientific study aims to compare two different techniques for placing nerve catheters used in pain management during shoulder surgeries. Peripheral regional anesthesia procedures have been established for decades as standard and particularly safe anesthesia techniques routinely applied in addition to general anesthesia for shoulder surgeries. These procedures help alleviate patients' pain during and, importantly, in the days following the operation, reducing the need for pain medication in tablet form or through intravenous administration. Consequently, side effects of pain medications (e.g., fatigue, nausea, constipation) can be avoided, and a faster rehabilitation process can be facilitated. Swift and as painless as possible mobilization is crucial for a positive outcome of shoulder surgeries. In the mentioned regional anesthesia procedure, the nerves originating from the cervical spine and supplying the shoulder are rinsed with a local anesthetic on the side of the neck. This interrupts pain transmission and perception for several hours. Simultaneously placing a nerve catheter to these nerves allows for extending this anesthesia as needed for several days after the operation. This is particularly beneficial postoperatively for pain-free execution of physiotherapeutic measures during these days, enhancing overall comfort.

The nerves supplying the shoulder and upper arm depart laterally from the spinal cord at the neck and form a nerve plexus (brachial plexus), which travels under the collarbone to the shoulder and arm. They mediate muscle movement and pain perception. Their anesthesia or the placement of a catheter into this nerve plexus occurs on the side of the neck, between two neck muscles in the so-called "scalene gap" through which the nerve plexus passes, making it very superficial and accessible for regional anesthesia. In the previously performed method, the nerve plexus at the neck is surrounded by a local anesthetic depot using an injection needle under ultrasound control. The thin (diameter <1 mm) nerve catheter is advanced a few centimeters beyond the needle into the depot and, after removing the needle, is secured at the skin by suturing. The final position of the catheter tip is not currently controlled with the conventional technique (A). Previous methods for monitoring have not gained widespread acceptance, despite about 25% of misplacements indicating the relevance of this problem, often leading to less effective or even absent pain therapy.

In this study, the conventional catheter placement technique (A) will be complemented with a color doppler ultrasound control (B) using an ultrasound device to compare both in terms of the success of pain therapy. Small amounts of saline solution will be injected through the catheter, and the doppler ultrasound will visualize the exit of these injections at the catheter tip in color on the ultrasound image, allowing the position of the catheter tip to be determined. Retractions and repeated doppler ultrasound controls until the catheter tip is at the desired target position allow for correction of initially misplaced catheters, presumably resulting in a better pain management outcome.
conditions: Intra- and postoperative pain following major shoulder surgeries

interventions.name: Peripheral regional anesthesia using color doppler ultrasound position control during interscalene catheter placement (ISC)
Peripheral regional anesthesia using conventionally ultrasound controlled placement during interscalene catheterization (ISC)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Major elective shoulder surgery
   -Consent for the establishment of a regional anesthesia procedure
   -Consent to participate in this study after comprehensive information provided by a study physician
Exclusion criteria:
- Age < 18 years
  - Lack of consent to participate in the study
   - Contraindications for peripheral regional anesthesia (e.g., allergies to local anesthetics, infections in the puncture area)
   - Chronic neurological deficit in the operated limb
   - Chronic pain syndrome or pain therapy (>6 months)
